records.name: DRY
records.why: Duplicate truth drifts. the sheet treats the embedded data object as the repeatable content owner.
records.directive: Execute DRY: one directive record owns name, expansion, why, anti-pattern, tags, and copy text; render cards, search, counts, and copy behavior from that source instead of duplicating content.
records.use: Directive records, source rows, prompt-pack variants, generated docs.
records.blocks: Changing a directive in the card but forgetting the search text, pack, source note, or count.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: KISS
records.why: the sheet improves the control spine without turning the sheet into a complex app.
records.directive: Execute KISS: preserve the single-file static artifact and existing UI mechanics; add the smallest meta-spine, stack, pack, and source updates that change agent behavior.
records.use: Static tools, prompt sheets, low-burden artifacts.
records.blocks: Framework migration, heavy UI rewrite, or clever generator before the data contract is extracted.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: YAGNI
records.why: Blocks speculative layers, future-proofing, unused providers, and extension points.
records.directive: Apply YAGNI: do not add features, providers, schemas, or extension points not required now.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: SSOT
records.why: The page now needs one canonical owner for each directive, source row, stack, pack, and note.
records.directive: Execute SSOT: keep each concept mastered in one data record; all visible cards, filters, counts, copy text, and source support should derive from or point back to that record.
records.use: Data-driven static pages, skill docs, generated prompt sheets.
records.blocks: Multiple inconsistent versions of the same directive scattered across sections.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: SRP
records.why: A module, function, skill, or workflow phase should have one clear reason to change.
records.directive: Apply SRP: separate parsing, validation, dispatch, execution, persistence, rendering, and reporting.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: SoC
records.why: Different concerns should be separated so one change does not cross-contaminate unrelated behavior.
records.directive: Apply SoC: separate policy, data, presentation, execution, verification, and reporting concerns.
records.blocks: Mixing UI, policy, persistence, and execution.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: IH
records.why: Hide volatile decisions behind stable interfaces so change stays local.
records.directive: Apply IH: expose the contract; hide representation, storage, algorithm, and provider details behind the owner.
records.blocks: Leaking implementation details into every caller.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: OCP
records.why: Extend behavior without editing stable core contracts when extension is expected and justified.
records.directive: Apply OCP only when extension is proven: keep stable core closed to churn and expose explicit extension seams.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: LoD
records.why: Minimize knowledge of internal object/module chains to reduce coupling.
records.directive: Apply LoD: talk to your direct owner/interface; do not reach through internals or patch deep private paths.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: LoP
records.why: Use the least expressive mechanism that can do the job; less power is easier to analyze and constrain.
records.directive: Apply Least Power: prefer data/config/schema/static HTML before code, code before agents, agents only when judgment is required.
records.blocks: Using a general agent where a schema or script would suffice.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: SLAP
records.why: Mixed abstraction levels make code and prompts hard to scan and maintain.
records.directive: Apply SLAP: keep each function, prompt block, or section at one abstraction level; extract lower-level detail.
records.use: Long prompts, functions, docs, and renderers with mixed policy/implementation detail.
records.blocks: Narrating strategy and low-level mechanics in the same block.
records.negative_example: invoking the acronym while violating the owner or evidence rule.

records.name: Interface Contract
records.why: APIs, CLIs, schemas, prompts, tools, and generated artifacts all have contracts.
records.directive: Preserve the contract. If it changes, update producers, consumers, tests, examples, and docs.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Owner First
records.why: Avoid downstream hacks that leave the real source wrong.
records.directive: OWNER FIRST: identify the owning file/module/schema/prompt before editing.
records.blocks: Editing generated output while source remains wrong.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: CC
records.why: Good modules have strong internal fit and weak external dependence.
records.directive: Maximize cohesion; minimize coupling. Move code/data/prompt rules until each unit has a clear internal purpose and few external reasons to change.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: DDD / BC
records.why: One model or term can mean different things in different contexts; boundaries prevent semantic drift.
records.directive: Use bounded contexts: define the local language, owners, translations, and integration seams before mixing models.
records.blocks: One global vocabulary that collapses distinct domains.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: SOLID
records.why: A familiar LLM-recognisable shorthand for keeping the artifact modular instead of becoming an acronym dump.
records.directive: Execute SOLID on the artifact: SRP separates stacks/cards/packs/sources/notes; OCP adds sections through data rather than renderer rewrites; LSP preserves card/pack/source shapes; ISP keeps search/copy/print controls narrow; DIP makes renderers depend on data contracts, not hard-coded content.
records.use: Artifact architecture, skill compilers, prompt-pack generators, UI/data separation.
records.blocks: A giant page where every new idea requires editing markup in multiple places.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: GRASP
records.why: GRASP answers the meta-question: who owns each responsibility in the sheet/build system?
records.directive: Execute GRASP: assign each responsibility to the information expert, keep card/prompt/source owners cohesive, keep coupling low through the JSON data contract, and use indirection only where it prevents drift.
records.use: Owner placement, renderer/data split, prompt-pack compilation, generated artifacts.
records.blocks: Putting behavior, source truth, and rendering responsibility in random downstream markup.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Ports & Adapters
records.why: Keep domain logic isolated from UI, databases, external APIs, and model providers.
records.directive: Use ports for domain needs and adapters for external details; test the core without network, filesystem, browser, or LLM dependencies.
records.blocks: Business logic trapped inside framework glue.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: CQRS
records.why: Reads and writes often need different models, permissions, and validation paths.
records.directive: Separate command paths from query paths when writes have different invariants, audit, authorization, or consistency needs.
records.blocks: One handler that both mutates and reports without clear guarantees.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Conway Check
records.why: System boundaries tend to reflect communication boundaries.
records.directive: Run a Conway Check: align module ownership, review paths, docs, and release process with the architecture you actually want.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Compatibility Matrix
records.why: Compatibility is not a feeling; it is a table of supported versions and surfaces.
records.directive: Maintain a compatibility matrix before changing producers or consumers: list supported versions, schemas, clients, prompt/skill formats, and generated artifacts; verify old and new examples pass or mark the break intentionally.
records.use: Releases, schema migrations, skills, generated artifacts, public APIs.
records.blocks: Silent mismatch between old consumers and new producers.
records.negative_example: updating the producer and discovering later that an old consumer parsed a field differently.

records.name: ADR
records.why: Important decisions need lightweight memory with tradeoffs and reversibility.
records.directive: Write an ADR when a structural choice changes owners, contracts, dependencies, or deployment shape.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: API First
records.why: A stable interface lets teams, tests, and agents reason before implementation details settle.
records.directive: Define examples, error cases, compatibility, and conformance tests before filling implementation internals.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: BFF
records.why: One backend shape rarely serves every client well without coupling or overfetching.
records.directive: Use BFF when client experiences diverge: give each frontend a thin backend adapter while keeping domain truth behind stable services.
records.blocks: Putting presentation-specific joins into core domain services.
records.negative_example: invoking the acronym while violating the owner or evidence rule.

records.name: ADR + RFC
records.expansion: Architecture Decision Record + Request for Comments
records.why: Decisions and normative contracts are different artifacts and should not be blurred.
records.directive: Use ADR for why a decision was made; use RFC/BCP-14 language for what implementations MUST/SHOULD/MAY do.
records.use: Architecture history, specs, prompt contracts, governance changes.
records.blocks: Embedding decision history inside normative requirements or vice versa.
records.negative_example: invoking the acronym while violating the owner or evidence rule.

records.name: ATAM
records.why: Architectures fail at quality-attribute tradeoffs long before syntax fails.
records.directive: Use ATAM for architecture choices with real tradeoffs: name quality attributes, candidate approaches, risks, sensitivity points, tradeoffs, and rejected options before choosing. Verify the decision lists risk owner, affected quality attributes, and evidence for the selected option.
records.use: Architecture decisions where security, modifiability, performance, availability, cost, or schedule compete.
records.blocks: Choosing architecture by preference, fashion, or single-metric optimization without recorded tradeoffs.
records.negative_example: selecting a platform because it is popular while omitting quality attributes, rejected options, and risk owner.

records.name: C4 Model
records.why: Different audiences need different architectural zoom levels.
records.directive: Use C4 when architecture discussion is too abstract: start with system context, then containers/components only as needed for the decision; stop before code-level detail unless the decision depends on it. Verify each box has a name, responsibility, boundary/owner, and relationship.
records.use: Architecture explanation, onboarding, design review, agent-generated diagrams, boundary disputes.
records.blocks: Jumping into code diagrams before actor, system, container, responsibility, and ownership boundaries are clear.
records.negative_example: drawing class boxes before naming external actors, system boundary, containers, and relationships.

records.name: SemVer
records.why: Consumers need release numbers that encode compatibility risk.
records.directive: Use SemVer before release/version changes: classify the diff as breaking, additive-compatible, or patch-level; choose major/minor/patch accordingly and block version bumps that understate compatibility impact. Verify release notes and tests match the classification.
records.use: Packages, APIs, schemas, prompt/skill releases, generated artifacts with consumers.
records.blocks: Version bumps that hide breaking changes, overstate compatibility, or make consumers guess upgrade risk.
records.negative_example: shipping a required-field contract change as a patch release because local tests passed.

records.name: Backward Compatibility
records.why: Compatibility has source, wire, and semantic dimensions; passing one does not prove the others.
records.directive: Before changing a consumed surface, check source, wire, and semantic compatibility: identify old consumers, old/new examples, migration path, and deprecation window. Stop if compatibility tests or a compatibility matrix are missing for supported consumers.
records.use: API evolution, schema migrations, CLI flags, agent skill releases, generated docs.
records.blocks: Breaking old clients through renamed fields, changed defaults, altered semantics, or undocumented output shifts.
records.negative_example: adding a required field to an existing request and calling it backward compatible without old-consumer tests.

records.name: Deprecation Policy
records.expansion: Safe removal path for supported behavior
records.why: Removal is a compatibility change with users, timelines, and evidence.
records.directive: Use a deprecation policy before removing or changing supported APIs, schemas, flags, prompt formats, or generated outputs: name replacement, notice, timeline, compatibility window, telemetry/usage signal, and final removal condition. Stop if consumers cannot migrate safely.
records.use: API evolution, schema/output changes, skill/prompt versioning, generated artifacts, CLI flags.
records.blocks: Surprise removals, silent breaking changes, and unsupported consumers discovering the break in production.
records.negative_example: deleting a field because no current test uses it while supported clients still may.

records.name: ACID
records.why: Generated artifacts can fail halfway just like data writes; the sheet treats file generation as a transaction.
records.directive: Execute ACID for artifact writes: generate to a new file, preserve a valid old version, validate JSON/HTML structure, avoid partial mutation, and report exactly what is unverified.
records.use: HTML generation, migrations, releases, source-table updates.
records.blocks: Overwriting the only working artifact with a broken half-generation.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: BASE
records.expansion: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
records.why: A useful contrast to ACID when distributed availability is the real tradeoff.
records.directive: Use BASE deliberately: state what may be stale, how it converges, and what users/tools must not assume during convergence.
records.blocks: Pretending eventual consistency is immediate correctness.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: CAP
records.why: For distributed state, failures force tradeoffs; do not promise all three under partition.
records.directive: Run a CAP check: identify what happens under partition, what becomes unavailable, and what can become stale.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Atomics
records.why: Find the smallest units that compose behavior: schema rows, handlers, prompts, fixtures, tests.
records.directive: Work from atomics upward: identify primitive owners first, then compose; do not patch only the surface output.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Atomic Patch
records.why: Code/schema/tests/docs should land as one coherent unit.
records.directive: Make the patch atomic: update every required producer, consumer, test, and doc together or mark the gap explicitly.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Idempotence
records.why: Critical for scripts, migrations, generated files, deployments, retries, and cleanup.
records.directive: Make retried work idempotent: rerunning a script, migration, generator, cleanup, or API write must detect prior completion and avoid duplicate side effects. Verify with a second run or dry-run that state is unchanged except for intended receipts.
records.use: Scripts, migrations, generators, deployments, retries, cleanup, tool writes.
records.blocks: Rerun damage, duplicate records, repeated messages, corrupted generated files, and drift after retry.
records.negative_example: a retry creates a second payment, ticket, migration row, or generated section.

records.name: Idempotency Key
records.expansion: One operation identity for retryable writes
records.why: Retries are necessary, but duplicate side effects are not.
records.directive: Use an idempotency key before retrying non-idempotent writes or tool actions: generate one stable operation ID, persist the first result, return the same result for duplicate attempts, and reject conflicting reuse. Verify duplicate requests do not create duplicate side effects.
records.use: HTTP/API writes, payment/order/ticket creation, queued jobs, tool calls, browser actions with retry.
records.blocks: Retry storms creating duplicate records, messages, charges, external actions, or inconsistent receipts.
records.negative_example: using a timestamp or random retry body so every retry looks like a new operation.

records.name: Invariants
records.why: Hard conditions prevent vague correctness claims.
records.directive: State the invariants before editing; verify the patch preserves or enforces each one.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Outbox Pattern
records.why: State changes and external messages should not split into inconsistent reality.
records.directive: Use an outbox: commit state and pending message together, then deliver externally with retry/idempotence.
records.blocks: DB updated but event/email/tool call lost.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: FIFO
records.why: Order matters for queues, migrations, task logs, and audit receipts.
records.directive: Use FIFO when order is part of correctness; document where reordering is allowed.
records.blocks: Assuming order from systems that do not guarantee it.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: RTO/RPO
records.expansion: Recovery Time Objective / Recovery Point Objective
records.why: Recovery needs time/data-loss targets, not just backup vibes.
records.directive: Define RTO/RPO before high-risk writes: how fast to restore and how much data loss is acceptable.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: PACELC
records.why: CAP is not enough; normal operation still trades latency against consistency.
records.directive: Apply PACELC: under partition decide A/C; otherwise decide L/C, then document the tradeoff.
records.use: Distributed state, queues, caches, sync, data contracts.
records.blocks: Claiming “CAP” while ignoring latency/consistency tradeoffs outside partitions.
records.negative_example: invoking the acronym while violating the owner or evidence rule.

records.name: Canonicalization
records.why: Avoid path, key, name, casing, Unicode, and notation drift.
records.directive: Canonicalize names, paths, schema keys, IDs, encodings, and notations before comparing, routing, or documenting.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: IR
records.why: Structured state between surface wording and execution.
records.directive: Route through IR: convert surface input into typed internal state before dispatching or answering.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: AST
records.why: A tree representation makes structure explicit before interpretation or transformation.
records.directive: Parse to an AST before modifying syntax-like content; transform nodes, not fragile text substrings.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: CFG
records.why: Execution order and branches should be visible before changing behavior.
records.directive: Sketch or inspect the CFG when bugs depend on branching, loops, early returns, retries, or stop conditions.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: SSA
records.why: A useful mental model for tracking where values are defined and transformed.
records.directive: Track each value definition once: name where data enters, mutates, branches, and reaches output.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Parse, Don’t Validate
records.why: Represent only valid states instead of accepting anything and checking later.
records.directive: Parse into typed objects that make invalid states unrepresentable; validate at the boundary, then trust the internal type.
records.blocks: Boolean flags and loose dictionaries everywhere.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Schema Gate
records.why: Machine-checkable contracts prevent prompt/schema drift.
records.directive: Validate input and output against schema before dispatch, persistence, or release.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Lowering
records.why: Separate intent from executable operations.
records.directive: Lower abstract requests into concrete operations with permissions, arguments, owners, and rollback before execution.
records.blocks: Letting prose directly call powerful tools.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Normal Form
records.why: A normal form makes equality, diffing, caching, and routing tractable.
records.directive: Normalize before diffing: sort keys, canonicalize paths, unify casing, stabilize whitespace, and fix encoding.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Phase Separation
records.why: Prevents semantic leakage between layers.
records.directive: Keep phases separate; dispatch only from validated state and render only what execution proves.
records.blocks: Rendering claims before execution proves them.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: HTML First
records.why: HTML defines structure and meaning; CSS and JS should enhance it.
records.directive: Start with semantic HTML: headings, landmarks, labels, buttons, links, forms, tables, and text that work before decoration.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: WCAG
records.why: Accessibility is a testable web contract, not optional polish.
records.directive: Apply WCAG: check perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust behavior before claiming UI quality.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: POUR
records.why: The WCAG mental model is highly LLM-recognisable and concise.
records.directive: Use POUR as the accessibility pass: can users perceive it, operate it, understand it, and rely on assistive interpretation?
records.blocks: Treating contrast as the whole of accessibility.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: a11y
records.why: Common shorthand that prompts LLMs toward accessible design checks.
records.directive: Run an a11y smoke: keyboard navigation, focus order, contrast, labels, alt text, reduced motion, and screen-reader landmarks.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: i18n / l10n
records.why: English-primary pages still need safe handling of language, direction, encoding, dates, and names.
records.directive: Apply i18n/l10n hygiene: UTF-8, lang attributes, dir/RTL support, locale-aware dates/numbers, and font fallback.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: RTL / BiDi
records.why: Mixed Arabic/Hebrew/English can visually reorder in confusing ways.
records.directive: Use dir, bdi, unicode-bidi, and isolated spans for mixed-direction text; visually smoke-test Arabic/English examples.
records.use: Islamic terms, Arabic names, multilingual docs.
records.blocks: Broken names, quotes, and symbols in RTL contexts.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: PE
records.why: Baseline content/functionality comes first; enhanced experience layers on top.
records.directive: Apply PE: content works without JS, then CSS and JS progressively improve interaction.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: RWD
records.why: Layouts must adapt to viewport, input mode, and print/PDF.
records.directive: Apply RWD: test small/mobile, wide desktop, zoom, print, and long text wrapping.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Mobile First
records.expansion: Small constraints expose content and interaction priorities.
records.why: Small constraints expose content and interaction priorities.
records.directive: Design mobile first, then enhance layout for larger screens; avoid hiding core content behind hover or wide tables.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: ARIA Last
records.why: ARIA can repair gaps but bad ARIA can make accessibility worse.
records.directive: Prefer native elements first; add ARIA only when semantics cannot be expressed natively and test the result.
records.blocks: Slapping ARIA on divs instead of using buttons/labels.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Feature Detection
records.why: The web varies by browser, device, extension, settings, and user preference.
records.directive: Use feature detection and graceful fallback; do not assume one browser or modern capability.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Content First
records.why: A sheet’s value is its scannable content; layout should reduce cognitive load.
records.directive: Prioritize content hierarchy, searchable labels, copyable directives, and print/PDF clarity before decoration.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: TDD
records.why: Write the failing expectation before the code when behavior is clear.
records.directive: Use TDD when the target behavior is known: red test, minimal green, refactor with tests still green.
records.blocks: Coding without an objective pass/fail target.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: BDD
records.why: Name behavior in user/scenario terms before implementation details.
records.directive: Use BDD for workflow behavior: Given state, When action, Then observable result.
records.blocks: Implementation tests that miss user-visible behavior.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Unit Test
records.why: The smallest useful proof for one unit’s behavior.
records.directive: Add or run a unit test when one function/module/handler owns the behavior.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Integration Test
records.why: Bugs often live where modules, services, tools, or schemas meet.
records.directive: Run integration tests for producer/consumer boundaries, tool calls, persistence, and schema exchange.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: E2E
records.why: Validates the user/workflow path across the full stack.
records.directive: Use E2E sparingly for critical flows; keep it stable, meaningful, and backed by lower-level tests.
records.blocks: Slow flaky suites as the only proof.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: PBT
records.why: Generate many inputs to test invariants, not just examples.
records.directive: Use PBT when invariants matter: define properties, generate inputs, shrink failures, and save counterexamples.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: MT
records.why: When exact oracle is hard, test relations across transformed inputs.
records.directive: Use MT: define metamorphic relations that should hold after input changes, reruns, reordering, or equivalent rewrites.
records.blocks: Giving up because expected exact output is hard.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Mutation Testing
records.why: If small code mutations survive, your tests may not guard the behavior.
records.directive: Use mutation checks for critical logic: introduce small changes and ensure tests fail for meaningful defects.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Golden Master
records.expansion: Capture existing behavior before changing it
records.why: Useful when legacy behavior must be preserved before refactor.
records.directive: Capture current behavior before refactor: save representative outputs, rerun after the change, and approve every delta as intentional or failed. Stop if the baseline cannot be reproduced.
records.use: Legacy code, generated artifacts, parser/compiler behavior, risky refactors.
records.blocks: Refactoring blind and mistaking accidental behavior drift for improvement.
records.negative_example: refactoring a generator without saving the before-output and then hand-waving a giant diff.

records.name: Golden Eval Set
records.why: Agent and prompt regressions need repeatable examples, not memory of what worked once.
records.directive: Maintain a golden eval set for prompt/skill/agent changes: include representative success, failure, adversarial, long-context, and source-conflict cases; rerun before claiming improvement. Stop if the changed behavior is not measured against the baseline.
records.use: Prompt packs, skills, agent harnesses, tool policies, generated artifacts with behavior expectations.
records.blocks: Vibe-tuned prompts, regressions hidden by a single demo, and improvements that cannot be reproduced.
records.negative_example: declaring a prompt better because one fresh example looked good.

records.name: Characterization Test
records.expansion: Describe what the system currently does
records.why: A safety net for code whose intended behavior is unclear.
records.directive: Add characterization tests before changing legacy or unclear code; later split intended behavior from discovered quirks.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Contract Test
records.why: Contracts must be executable, not merely documented.
records.directive: Add contract tests for APIs, schemas, tool definitions, prompt outputs, and generated artifacts.
records.blocks: Docs say one thing, consumer receives another.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Smoke Test
records.why: Prevents plausible but untested completions.
records.directive: Run the smallest meaningful test/check and report the command plus result before claiming completion.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: RTFM
records.why: No guessing from memory when files, docs, logs, schemas, or tests exist.
records.directive: RTFM: inspect the governing files and relevant docs before editing or claiming.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: TRACE
records.why: Prevents vibe patches and false fixes.
records.directive: TRACE BEFORE CHANGE: identify call path, data path, owner, and test surface before patching.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Define Done
records.why: Completion should be objective.
records.directive: Define done: list success criteria before acting; do not claim completion until each is passed or marked unverified.
records.negative_example: applying the label while skipping the owner, evidence, or stop condition.

records.name: Plan + Persist
records.why: Good for multi-step work where agents stop too early.

records.directive: Apply CUPID: prefer composable, predictable, idiomatic, domain-shaped units over clever abstractions.
records.use: Library/API design, agent tool surfaces, reusable modules.
records.blocks: Rigid SOLID theater that makes systems less usable.
records.negative_example: invoking the acronym while violating the owner or evidence rule.
